article_content: At this year’s Consumer Electronics Show, the buzz isn’t just about bigger screens or faster chips—it’s about tiny sensors quietly observing every part of your day. From your dinner plate to your suitcase, technology is stepping in to track, nudge, and manage the mundane. One standout? The HAPIfork, a clever utensil designed by French engineer Jacques Lepine after his family teased him for scarfing down meals. This isn’t just a fork—it vibrates and flashes if you’re eating too fast, helping you slow down, digest better, and maybe even shed a few pounds. It syncs with an app to log your eating habits, and yes, a matching HAPIspoon is in development. Priced at $99, it’ll hit shelves in April after a February Kickstarter launch. Meanwhile, Lowe’s Iris system aims to be the brain behind your smart home. Instead of juggling ten different apps for lights, thermostats, and pet doors, Iris unifies them all into one dashboard. You can get alerts when your back door swings open, monitor your plants’ moisture, or even keep tabs on an aging relative’s home with emergency buttons and anomaly detection. Partners like Verizon, Whirlpool, and PetSafe are adding more sensors soon. For travelers tired of lost bags, Trakdot offers peace of mind. This palm-sized tracker slips into your suitcase, uses a built-in SIM card to report location via text or app, and automatically enters sleep mode during flight to comply with FAA rules. At $50 plus a small annual fee, it’s a small price for knowing your luggage isn’t stuck in Frankfurt. Canopy’s Sensus case turns your iPhone into a touch-sensitive playground—not just the screen, but the sides and back too. Gamers and power users might love the extra controls, though it’ll need more apps to truly shine. And for those ready to ditch their phone and wear their interface, Vuzix’s M100 smart glasses deliver Android-powered calls, video, and navigation right on your lenses. With GPS, Bluetooth, and 720p recording, they’re aiming for a summer release across iOS and Android.

Por US$ 50 mais uma pequena taxa anual, é um preço pequeno para saber que sua mala não está presa em Frankfurt. O estojo Sensus da Canopy transforma seu iPhone em um playground sensível ao toque—não só a tela, mas também os lados e costas. Jogadores e usuários avançados podem adorar os controles extras, embora ele precise de mais aplicativos para realmente brilhar. E para quem está pronto para largar o telefone e usar sua interface nos olhos, os óculos inteligentes Vuzix M100 oferecem chamadas, vídeos e navegação impulsionados por Android diretamente na sua visão. Com GPS, Bluetooth e gravação em 720p, eles visam um lançamento no verão para iOS e Android.

article_content: In Lubbock County, Texas, County Judge Tom Head sparked national outrage after suggesting during a public interview that a second term for President Obama could trigger civil war — claiming the president might deploy United Nations troops to disarm American citizens. Head, whose duties include emergency planning, maintained his comments were intended as a hypothetical worst-case scenario, not a forecast. Still, his remarks — broadcast on local TV and radio — prompted immediate condemnation from Democrats and unease among many Republicans. Kenny Ketner, the newly appointed head of the Lubbock County Democratic Party, demanded Head’s resignation, calling his statements dangerous and unbecoming of an elected official. Carl Tepper, the county Republican chair, refused to endorse the views but upheld Head’s right to express them, noting that respectful disagreement doesn’t negate democratic representation. Sheriff Kelly Rowe confirmed no discussions had taken place about mobilizing against UN forces, and Gilbert Flores, the sole Democrat on the county commission, bluntly described Head as 'a six-pack short of a full case of beer.' A handful of residents praised Head for his staunch defense of gun rights and distrust of federal power, while others, including attorney Rod Hobson, responded with satire — placing UN flags outside his office to underscore the absurdity. Though Head later clarified he didn’t believe such a scenario was likely, his fusion of theological conviction with public office raised concerns among voters and officials alike. With control over millions in taxpayer dollars, many questioned how such extreme rhetoric aligns with responsible governance — while the episode highlighted growing tensions in America’s political landscape.

article_content: The federal lawsuit filed by Pennsylvania Governor Tom Corbett on behalf of the state against the NCAA is politically savvy — but legally indefensible. It is never unpopular for a state leader to defend the flagship university, particularly when that leader faces scrutiny over his role in delaying the investigation into Jerry Sandusky. Yet legally, the suit is deeply flawed. Recall the context: In the wake of the national scandal surrounding Sandusky’s crimes, Penn State University agreed to a settlement with the NCAA to resolve allegations of failing to supervise its football program. The terms were severe: a $60 million fine, a four-year ban on scholarships and bowl appearances, and relaxed transfer rules allowing athletes to leave without penalty. Meanwhile, criminal proceedings against university administrators for perjury and failure to report abuse continue separately. Like most plea deals, the settlement benefited both sides. For Penn State, it avoided a lengthy, public NCAA infractions process that could have kept Sandusky’s crimes and Joe Paterno’s controversial legacy in the headlines indefinitely. Worse, the NCAA’s infractions committee might have imposed the dreaded 'death penalty' — a multi-year shutdown of the football program — a consequence far more devastating than the agreed sanctions. Crucially, Penn State agreed in the settlement not to challenge the NCAA’s authority in court. Governor Corbett, however, has called the sanctions 'overreaching and unlawful,' and other lawmakers have objected to the fine being used to fund programs in other states. While Pennsylvania was not bound by the settlement and thus technically eligible to sue, that very fact undermines the lawsuit’s legitimacy. The suit seeks an injunction to block the NCAA from enforcing the sanctions. But injunctions require proof that irreparable harm is imminent. What harm will Pennsylvania suffer? The state partially funds Penn State. Therefore, the complaint argues, state funds will indirectly be drained as Penn State pays fines. But this is illogical: Pennsylvania is essentially claiming it will be hurt by its own choice to fund the university. If the state truly wants to avoid financial loss, it could simply halt funding during the sanction period — yet it has not. The real victims cited in the complaint — local businesses, students, ticket holders, vendors — lack legal standing to sue. Their inclusion reveals the state’s desperation: it’s appealing to emotion, not law. The complaint reads more like a campaign ad than a legal filing, praising Penn State’s educational values and painting the NCAA as greedy and conspiratorial. It even criticizes the NCAA president’s salary as a 'substantial raise' over his predecessor’s — irrelevant to the legal merits. This lawsuit will likely be dismissed on a motion to dismiss. Its highest point is already behind it — the media attention. But suppose Pennsylvania wins. What then? The NCAA can simply reopen the case and pursue the infractions process — potentially triggering the death penalty. If Joe Paterno were still alive, he’d say: Sometimes, it’s smarter to punt.
translated_content: A ação judicial federal apresentada pelo governador da Pensilvânia, Tom Corbett, em nome do estado contra a NCAA é politicamente astuta — mas juridicamente insustentável. Nunca é impopular para um líder estadual defender a universidade principal, especialmente quando esse líder enfrenta escrutínio por seu papel em atrasar a investigação sobre Jerry Sandusky. Contudo, juridicamente, o processo é profundamente falho. Lembre-se do contexto: Na esteira do escândalo nacional em torno dos crimes de Sandusky, a Universidade da Pensilvânia concordou com um acordo com a NCAA para resolver alegações de falha na supervisão de seu programa de futebol americano. Os termos foram severos: uma multa de 60 milhões de dólares, uma proibição de quatro anos de bolsas e aparições em jogos de pós-temporada, e regras relaxadas permitindo que atletas deixassem a universidade sem penalidades. Enquanto isso, processos criminais contra administradores universitários por perjúrio e falha em relatar abuso continuam separadamente. Como a maioria dos acordos de culpabilidade, o acordo beneficiou ambos os lados. Para a Pensilvânia, evitou um processo prolongado e público da NCAA que poderia ter mantido os crimes de Sandusky e o legado controverso de Joe Paterno nos holofotes por mais tempo. Pior ainda, o comitê de infrações da NCAA poderia ter imposto o temido 'penalty da morte' — um encerramento por vários anos do programa de futebol americano — uma consequência muito mais devastadora do que as sanções acordadas. Crucialmente, a Universidade da Pensilvânia concordou no acordo em não desafiar a autoridade da NCAA em tribunal. O governador Corbett, contudo, chamou as sanções de 'excessivas e ilegais', e outros legisladores se opuseram ao uso da multa para financiar programas em outros estados. Embora a Pensilvânia não estivesse vinculada ao acordo e, portanto, tecnicamente elegível para processar, esse exato fato mina a legitimidade da ação judicial. O processo busca uma injunção para impedir a NCAA de aplicar as sanções. Mas injunções exigem prova de que um dano irreparável está iminente. Que dano a Pensilvânia sofrerá? O estado financia parcialmente a Universidade da Pensilvânia. Portanto, a queixa argumenta que os fundos estaduais serão indiretamente esgotados à medida que a Universidade paga as multas. Mas isso é ilógico: a Pensilvânia está basicamente afirmando que será prejudicada por sua própria escolha de financiar a universidade. Se o estado realmente quiser evitar perda financeira, poderia simplesmente interromper o financiamento durante o período de sanção — porém, não o fez. As vítimas reais citadas na queixa — negócios locais, estudantes, titulares de ingressos, fornecedores — não têm legitimidade para processar. Sua inclusão revela a desesperança do estado: está apelando para a emoção, não para a lei. A queixa parece mais um comercial de campanha do que um documento jurídico, elogiando os valores educacionais da Universidade da Pensilvânia e pintando a NCAA como gananciosa e conspiratória. Ela até critica o salário do presidente da NCAA como um 'aumento substancial' em relação ao seu antecessor — irrelevante para os méritos legais. Essa ação judicial provavelmente será descartada em uma moção de extinção. Seu ponto mais alto já passou — a atenção da mídia. Mas suponha que a Pensilvânia vença. E daí? A NCAA pode simplesmente reabrir o caso e buscar o processo de infrações — potencialmente desencadeando o penalty da morte. Se Joe Paterno ainda estivesse vivo, ele diria: Às vezes, é mais sábio fazer um 'punt'.

article_content: Montreal police have formally charged 29-year-old Luka Rocco Magnotta with first-degree murder in the horrific killing and dismemberment of Jun Lin, a 33-year-old Chinese student at Concordia University. Authorities believe Lin was killed in late May inside a Montreal apartment, and his body was later cut apart and disposed of — one hand and foot sent by mail to federal political offices in Ottawa, and a torso discarded in a building’s dumpster. Magnotta, who goes by aliases including Eric Clinton Newman and Vladimir Romanov, is believed to have recorded the attack and uploaded a graphic 10-minute video online. Police say he sought fame through shock, calling him 'very deranged' and motivated by attention. Beyond murder, Magnotta faces charges related to distributing obscene material, sending indecent items through the mail, and desecrating human remains. A fifth charge alleges he threatened Canada’s Prime Minister Stephen Harper and members of Parliament, likely in retaliation for the political parties receiving the body parts. After fleeing Canada for Europe, Magnotta triggered a global manhunt led by Interpol. Investigators suspect he may be hiding in Eastern Europe, possibly due to his use of a Russian pseudonym and content on his multilingual website, which features Arabic and Russian text alongside provocative photos. Before this case, Magnotta was known to online animal rights communities as the 'Vacuum Kitten Killer' — linked to videos showing cats being drowned and suffocated. Activists had been tracking him for over a year and shared evidence with Canadian police. Magnotta denies wrongdoing, claiming on his website that he is the target of fake sites using his image to spread lies. Police, however, remain convinced his need for notoriety will ultimately betray him. Described as 5'8'', 135 lbs, with black hair and blue eyes, he remains at large — but authorities say it’s only a matter of time before he’s found.

Antes deste caso, Magnotta era conhecido entre comunidades online de direitos animais como o 'Vacuum Kitten Killer', ligado a vídeos em que gatos eram afogados e sufocados. Ativistas o rastreavam há mais de um ano e repassaram evidências às autoridades canadenses. article_content: WASHINGTON (CNN) — A bloody war between Mexican drug cartels is no longer solely a problem south of the border, members of Congress said Tuesday during a hearing on the issue. A member of the Mexican Federal Police patrols in Ciudad Juárez during a recent anti-drug operation. The violence accompanying these battles has spread into the United States and is largely fueled by money and firearms originating in America, said Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Illinois, chairman of the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Drugs. 'The drugs are coming north, and we're sending money and guns south,' Durbin said. 'As a result, these cartels have gained extraordinary power.' According to the federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), about 90% of guns seized in Mexican raids are traced back to the United States. The Brookings Institution estimates that roughly 2,000 firearms cross the border into Mexico daily. The subcommittee held a joint hearing with the Senate Caucus on International Narcotics Control, focusing on how the U.S. can support Mexican President Felipe Calderón’s efforts to combat drug-related violence. American communities are also seeing increased violent crime linked to the Mexican drug trade. In Phoenix, Arizona, in 2008, 366 kidnappings for ransom were reported — more than in any other U.S. city, Durbin said, citing federal data. The vast majority, he added, were tied to Mexican cartels. 'We're not winning the battle,' said Arizona Attorney General Terry Goddard. 'The violence we see in Mexico is fueled 65 to 70 percent by the trade in one drug: marijuana.' Goddard believes the U.S. can do more to eliminate profits from these operations and reduce domestic drug demand. The influence of cartels extends beyond border states. Durbin noted that authorities believe cartels now operate in 230 U.S. cities, up from 50 in 2006. In his home state of Illinois — far from the Mexican border — cartels are believed active in Chicago, East St. Louis, and Joliet. Lawmakers and witnesses universally praised Calderón’s efforts, including deploying troops to Ciudad Juárez. 'I think he needs every single bit of our support,' said Sen. Dianne Feinstein, D-California. Yet violence has surged, Goddard warned, with a disturbing new trend: assassinations of police officers, prosecutors, and other officials fighting cartels. Even more alarming, innocent civilians are increasingly at risk. In one Phoenix case, criminals carrying out a home invasion targeted the wrong house. 'The casual fallout will be significant if we can't do something to help Mexico stop this south of the border,' Goddard said. Arizona authorities have intercepted wire transfers to smugglers, seizing $17 million between 2003 and 2007. But a broader, regional strategy is needed, he emphasized, since cartels shift operations when pressured in one area. Authorities must target the leaders behind the violence, not just low-level operatives, he added: 'Arresting and deporting low-level operatives is a waste of critical resources.' Also Tuesday, a federal firearms official told the subcommittee of a 'troubling increase' in hand grenades seized from Mexican traffickers. William Hoover of the ATF expressed concern that explosives-related violence could spill over into U.S. border towns. 'In the past six months, we've noted a troubling rise in grenades seized from or used by drug traffickers,' Hoover said. He did not provide exact numbers, and ATF had no immediate statistics available. Meanwhile, Anthony Placido of the Drug Enforcement Administration told lawmakers he does not expect cartels to deliberately target U.S. officials, government interests, or civilians in the near term. 'Defining spillover is a tricky business,' he added. CNN Homeland Security Correspondents Jeanne Meserve, Mike M. Ahlers, and Carol Cratty contributed to this report.
translated_content: WASHINGTON (CNN) — Uma guerra sangrenta entre os cartéis mexicanos de drogas já não é mais apenas um problema ao sul da fronteira, disseram membros do Congresso na terça-feira durante uma audiência sobre o assunto. Um membro da Polícia Federal Mexicana patrulha em Ciudad Juárez durante uma operação recente contra o tráfico. A violência que acompanha esses conflitos se espalhou pelos Estados Unidos e é amplamente alimentada por dinheiro e armas provenientes dos EUA, disse o senador Dick Durbin, D-Illinois, presidente da Subcomissão de Crimes e Drogas do Senado. 'As drogas estão vindo para o norte, e nós estamos enviando dinheiro e armas para o sul,' disse Durbin. 'Como resultado, esses cartéis adquiriram poder extraordinário.' Segundo o Escritório Federal de Álcool, Tabaco, Armas de Fogo e Explosivos (ATF), cerca de 90% das armas apreendidas em operações mexicanas são rastreadas até os Estados Unidos. A instituição Brookings estima que cerca de 2.000 armas de fogo cruzam a fronteira para o México diariamente. A subcomissão realizou uma audiência conjunta com o Caucos do Senado para Narcóticos Internacionais, focando em como os EUA podem apoiar os esforços do presidente mexicano Felipe Calderón para combater a violência relacionada às drogas. Comunidades americanas também estão enfrentando um aumento da criminalidade violenta ligada ao tráfico mexicano. Em Phoenix, Arizona, em 2008, foram relatados 366 sequestros por resgate — mais do que em qualquer outra cidade dos EUA, disse Durbin, citando dados federais. A grande maioria, acrescentou ele, estava ligada aos cartéis mexicanos. 'Nós não estamos ganhando a batalha,' disse o procurador-geral do Arizona, Terry Goddard. 'A violência que vemos no México é impulsionada em 65 a 70% pelo comércio de uma droga: maconha.' Goddard acredita que os EUA podem fazer mais para eliminar os lucros dessas operações e reduzir a demanda interna por drogas. A influência dos cartéis se estende além dos estados fronteiriços. Durbin observou que autoridades acreditam que os cartéis agora atuam em 230 cidades americanas, contra 50 em 2006. No seu estado natal, Illinois — longe da fronteira mexicana — acredita-se que os cartéis operem em Chicago, East St. Louis e Joliet. Legisladores e testemunhas elogiaram universalmente os esforços de Calderón, incluindo o envio de tropas a Ciudad Juárez. 'Eu acho que ele precisa de todo o nosso apoio,' disse a senadora Dianne Feinstein, D-Califórnia. Contudo, a violência aumentou drasticamente, alertou Goddard, com uma nova tendência alarmante: assassinatos de policiais, promotores e outros funcionários que combatem os cartéis. Ainda mais assustador, à medida que a violência aumenta, cresce a possibilidade de cidadãos inocentes serem atingidos. Em um caso em Phoenix, criminosos em uma invasão domiciliar erraram a casa. 'O dano colateral será significativo se não fizermos algo para ajudar o México a parar isso ao sul da fronteira,' disse Goddard. Autoridades do Arizona interceptaram transferências bancárias para contrabandistas de drogas e pessoas, apreendendo US$ 17 milhões entre 2003 e 2007. Mas é necessária uma estratégia mais abrangente e regional, enfatizou ele, pois os cartéis simplesmente mudam suas operações quando pressionados em uma área. As autoridades devem atingir os líderes por trás da violência, e não apenas operários de baixo nível, acrescentou ele: 'Prender e deportar operários de baixo nível é um desperdício de recursos críticos.' Também na terça-feira, um funcionário federal de armas informou à subcomissão sobre um 'aumento preocupante' no número de granadas apreendidas de traficantes mexicanos recentemente. William Hoover, do ATF, expressou preocupação com a possibilidade de violência com explosivos se espalhar para cidades fronteiriças dos EUA. 'Nos últimos seis meses, notamos um aumento preocupante no número de granadas apreendidas de ou usadas por traficantes de drogas,' disse Hoover. Ele não forneceu estatísticas exatas, e o ATF não tinha dados imediatamente disponíveis. Enquanto isso, Anthony Placido, da Administração de Combate às Drogas, disse aos legisladores que não espera que os cartéis alvejem intencionalmente autoridades, interesses ou civis americanos no curto prazo. article_content: Beneath a simple gray stone marked '2008,' on a quiet slope at the Los Angeles County Crematory and Cemetery, rest the unclaimed remains of those who lived — and died — without family, resources, or a voice. On Wednesday morning, clergy gathered to offer a final blessing to 1,639 individuals who passed away in 2008 and were never claimed by loved ones. These solemn burials have occurred annually since 1896, when the county began serving as the last safety net for the destitute, the homeless, the addicted, and the isolated. Many could not afford cremation. Others lost family members too impoverished to pay for a funeral — a heartbreaking double loss. Last year, 1,698 unclaimed bodies were cremated here; the year before, 1,798. By law, the cemetery must wait three years before burying unclaimed remains. Stella Inouye, a financial services coordinator at the cemetery, noted that while cremation costs $352 for those who die in county hospitals and $466 elsewhere, families can apply for a fee waiver by submitting a hardship letter — yet many remain unaware. Around 15 people attended the ceremony — mostly volunteers and social workers from Skid Row, Los Angeles’ downtown homeless community. Jeff Dietrich of Hospitality Kitchen, which serves meals to the unhoused, said, 'These people may have eaten at our soup kitchen — or even shared our home. Their stories are untold, their connections severed. But in these final moments, we choose to be present.' Chaplain Chris Ponnet led the gathering, invoking sacred space for the nameless and forgotten. Clergy from Hindu, Buddhist, and Jewish traditions also offered blessings. Rambhoeu Brinkmann, speaking in the Hindu tradition, declared: 'This is a day of eternal life. For them, there will be all they wished for — and more, in our presence.' The ceremony ended quietly. The grave marker '2008' now rests adorned with a yellow ribbon and a modest bouquet of roses — a silent testament to dignity in death.

article_content: Following the Supreme Court’s invalidation of part of Arizona’s voter registration law, states should reconsider efforts to make voting more difficult. Monday’s ruling is a major win for voters—but it also underscores a sobering truth: free, fair, and accessible elections in the U.S. are far from guaranteed. To strengthen our democracy, we must modernize our election infrastructure. The Court affirmed Congress’s broad constitutional authority to regulate federal elections, especially as lawmakers in nearly two dozen states continue pushing measures that restrict voter access. Before the 2012 election, over 100 restrictive bills were introduced across 19 states. While many were blocked by courts or the Justice Department, the momentum persisted into 2013. This decision gives federal legislators a powerful foundation to establish minimum national voting standards and bring our system into the 21st century. Central to this effort is the National Voter Registration Act of 1993—the so-called 'Motor Voter' law. Designed to simplify registration, it allowed Americans to sign up by mail, during driver’s license applications, or at other government offices. The law succeeded: nearly 16 million people register annually using its methods, dramatically increasing participation. But in 2004, Arizona passed a law requiring documentary proof of citizenship for voter registration. This conflicted directly with the federal form, leading to the rejection of thousands of valid applications, hindering mail-in registration, and crippling community outreach efforts. The Supreme Court’s ruling explicitly prohibits such state-level interference. Yet, the Motor Voter law itself is now outdated. Born in an era of paper forms and postal delays, it still relies on handwritten applications prone to errors—misspelled names, illegible addresses—that contribute to long lines and Election Day confusion. These inefficiencies threaten both access and electoral integrity. We now have the tools to fix this. Digital solutions—such as secure online registration, automatic updates when citizens move, and integrated registration at DMVs or social service agencies—can register an additional 50 million eligible voters at lower cost and with fewer errors. Fraud risks are minimal compared to the scale of disenfranchisement caused by outdated systems. Progress is already underway. Colorado, Virginia, and West Virginia have launched online registration. In January 2014, Rep. John Lewis and Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the Voter Empowerment Act, which prioritizes modernization. But these efforts are fragmented. What we need is a unified, nationwide standard. The Court upheld a vital step—but it’s only the beginning. To ensure every eligible American can vote easily and reliably, voter registration must be fully digitized. The time to act is now.

article_content: Kim Kardashian has publicly reversed her support for the Hollywood boycott of The Beverly Hills Hotel, citing concern for the hotel’s staff rather than its owner, the Sultan of Brunei. The boycott was initiated in protest against Brunei’s introduction of Sharia law in April 2019, which mandates stoning as punishment for homosexual acts. In a heartfelt blog post titled 'My Thoughts,' the reality star explained that while she fully condemns the Sultan’s laws — which she says contradict everything she believes in — she no longer supports punishing the employees who have served her family for decades. 'For a sultan with $20 billion, this loss of business doesn’t even make a dent in his fortunes,' she wrote. 'But the hotel staff are being negatively affected every day.' Kim recalled visiting the hotel as a child with her father, Robert Kardashian, and forming lasting bonds with staff members who still work there today. During her pregnancy with daughter North West, she befriended a waitress who was also expecting; the two shared stories and milestones. 'I know for a fact she has a new baby at home that she has to feed,' Kim said. 'This boycott is affecting her tremendously.' She praised fellow celebrities Russell Crowe and Rose McGowan for taking similar stances — Crowe for opposing the boycott on ethical grounds, and McGowan for hosting a 'gay-in' cocktail party at the hotel to show solidarity with staff and the LGBTQ+ community. Kim affirmed her unwavering support for global LGBTQ+ rights, stating, 'The unjust treatment and violation of rights of the LGBT community around the world is never justified.' However, she urged for alternative forms of protest that don’t harm innocent workers. She welcomed efforts by industry leaders like Jeffrey Katzenberg and Casey Wasserman to engage with hotel management to find solutions. The Beverly Hills Hotel, a historic 102-year-old landmark, has committed to protecting employee wages, tips, and benefits amid the controversy. Kim concluded by asking the public to extend compassion to those who rely on the hotel for their livelihoods — 'not forgetting them during this protest.'

article_content: Sugary energy drinks may have cost athletes a gold medal at the Olympics, health experts have claimed. A new study found that toothache and bleeding gums affected nearly one-fifth of athletes’ performances at the London 2012 Games. Nagging oral pain could have made the difference between winning and losing by disrupting focus and physical rhythm. The survey revealed that 18% of elite athletes reported their oral health negatively impacted their performance. Toothache and bleeding gums may have cost athletes the distinction between silver and gold, as persistent discomfort throws them off their stride. Nearly half (46.5%) of the athletes surveyed had not visited a dentist in the past year. Saliva protects teeth from decay and erosion, but dehydration from intense training can cause dry mouth, increasing oral health risks. Athletes often consume high-carbohydrate diets and frequent sugary, acidic energy drinks to fuel performance—both of which contribute to tooth decay and enamel erosion. Dentists advise that simple habits—such as proper flossing, using fluoride toothpaste and mouthwash, and avoiding rinsing after brushing—can deliver marginal performance gains comparable to expensive physical therapies. A separate study by German researchers, published last month, found that the longer athletes train, the less saliva they produce—and the more alkaline it becomes. Alkaline saliva promotes plaque bacteria growth, accelerating tooth decay. For every additional hour of training per week, the risk of needing fillings or experiencing decayed or missing teeth rose significantly. Researchers suggest endurance exercise may reduce enamel-protecting proteins in saliva, meaning even water consumption could contribute to erosion. A team from the University Hospital Heidelberg examined the teeth of 35 triathletes and 35 non-athletes. Health experts at University College London argue that dentistry must be given equal priority to other sports sciences to optimize athletic potential. Professor Ian Needleman of UCL’s Eastman Dental Institute said: 'Oral health could be an easy win for athletes—conditions affecting performance are largely preventable. Professional teams invest heavily in tiny performance advantages. Simple, low-cost strategies like improved brushing technique and high-fluoride products can make the crucial difference between gold and silver.' He emphasized that water or hypotonic drinks are preferable for hydration, and urged athletes to spit out toothpaste rather than rinse after brushing. 'For sports requiring heavy energy drink use, high-fluoride toothpastes and mouthrinses should be seriously considered,' he added. The findings were published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine. Experts stress that while energy drinks are not to be demonized, athletes must be informed of their oral health risks and adopt simple protective measures.

article_content: Oranjestad, Aruba (CNN) — Aruban prosecutors plan to release on Tuesday the results of forensic tests conducted on a jawbone discovered on a beach, determining whether it belongs to missing U.S. teenager Natalee Holloway, officials said. The tests, carried out at the Netherlands Forensic Institute in The Hague, first sought to establish whether the bone was human or animal. If human, authorities planned to use DNA analysis to determine if it matched Holloway’s remains. The 18-year-old from Alabama vanished in 2005 after being last seen leaving an Oranjestad nightclub with Joran van der Sloot and two other men. She was in Aruba with about 100 classmates celebrating their graduation from Mountain Brook High School in suburban Birmingham, Alabama. Aruba’s Solicitor General, Taco Stein, confirmed prosecutors will issue a public statement Tuesday with the findings. Holloway’s dental records were submitted to the forensic institute last week, according to the FBI. Tim Miller, director of Texas EquuSearch — a nonprofit search-and-rescue group that has assisted in the hunt for Holloway — said her father, Dave Holloway, believes the bone is his daughter’s. 'Dave has been in contact with Aruban authorities and spoke with the FBI agent handling the case this morning. Dave believes it is Natalee,' Miller said. Attempts to reach Dave Holloway Monday were unsuccessful. Part of a jawbone with a tooth was found earlier this month by an American tourist near the Phoenix Hotel, a large resort on Aruba’s western coast, according to prosecutor Peter Blanken. The hotel referred all inquiries to local authorities. The bone was initially assessed by an Aruban forensic expert, who concluded it came from a young woman. However, Blanken emphasized that the final determination rests with the Netherlands Forensic Institute. On Monday, police collected a second bone found earlier this month on the same beach by a family from New Jersey, said Ana Angela, spokesperson for Aruban prosecutors. Richard Roy, general manager of the Westin Hotel, where the family was staying, said the bone 'does not appear to be human.' The family had placed the object on their hotel balcony. After hearing media reports about the first bone, they contacted the FBI and then the hotel. Hotel staff retrieved the item and alerted police. Van der Sloot was detained twice in connection with Holloway’s disappearance but never charged. He is now awaiting trial in Lima, Peru, for the murder of Peruvian student Stephany Flores, whose body was found in May in a hotel room registered to him. Surveillance footage showed the two entering the room together. Van der Sloot, 23, is also charged in Alabama with wire fraud and extortion for allegedly attempting to extort more than $250,000 from Holloway’s family in exchange for information about her whereabouts.

article_content: As floodwaters rise in New York City following a powerful storm surge, rats are being forced out of their underground burrows and into human spaces — raising concerns about disease transmission, according to Rick Ostfeld, an ecologist at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in Milbrook, New York. Torrents of water inundated subways, road tunnels, and city streets, prompting rats — skilled swimmers and climbers — to seek higher ground in apartments and buildings. Ostfeld told The Huffington Post that these rodents are highly adaptable survivors, capable of thriving in disturbed environments. Their movement into new areas could lead to increased exposure to dangerous pathogens, including leptospirosis, hantavirus, typhus, salmonella, and even plague. Importantly, transmission does not require bites; human contact with contaminated urine or feces is sufficient to spread these illnesses. Ostfeld emphasized that rats live in complex social groups, and sudden displacement could destabilize their populations, driving them into regions they’ve never infested before. 'One of the things we know can exacerbate disease is massive dispersal,' he said. Historical precedents exist: earlier this year in the UK, flood-driven rat displacement led to widespread infestations in homes. While the sheer volume of water from the storm may dilute some pathogens — potentially lowering immediate risk — experts warn that the disruption itself poses a serious public health concern. 'It’s not just about the high winds and rain,' Ostfeld noted. 'A rat disturbance is something we should be concerned about.'

article_content: Many of the world’s most important crop-producing countries could be fully saturated with pests by mid-century if current trends continue, according to a study. More than one in ten pest types are already present in around half the countries that grow their host crops. If this spread continues at its current rate, scientists warn that a significant proportion of global crop-producing nations will be overwhelmed by pests within the next 30 years. Research from the University of Exeter indicates that a warming planet is altering the distribution of crop pests. The study projects that many countries could face pest saturation by 2050, posing a grave threat to global food security. The root knot nematode (Meloidogyne incognita) on a tomato plant is one example of the pests driving this trend. The findings were published in the journal Global Ecology and Biogeography. British researchers have also demonstrated that genetically modified insects could eliminate fruit fly pests damaging crops such as oranges, peaches, apples, and pears. Earlier this year, scientists created genetically modified male Mediterranean fruit flies using technology developed by the UK bioscience company Oxitec. These GM males carry a gene that causes female offspring to die before reaching maturity, reducing the overall population of fruit flies and minimizing crop damage. Oxitec promotes this approach as a chemical-free alternative to pesticides, aiming to increase crop yields. The company has engaged with UK government agencies to conduct field trials. The study analyzes global pest distribution patterns using databases to assess factors influencing how many countries pests reach and how many species occur per country. Crop pests include fungi, bacteria, viruses, insects, nematodes, viroids, and oomycetes. Dr. Dan Bebber of the University of Exeter’s Biosciences Department stated: 'If crop pests continue to spread at current rates, many of the world’s biggest crop-producing nations will be inundated by mid-century, posing a grave threat to global food security.' The study identifies several highly invasive pests likely to expand in coming decades—including three tropical root knot nematode species that infect thousands of plant species, Blumeria graminis (a fungus causing powdery mildew on cereals), and the Citrus tristeza virus. Named for the 'sadness' it brings to citrus growers in Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking regions, the Citrus tristeza virus had spread to 105 of 145 citrus-growing countries by 2000. Fungi lead the global invasion of crops, being the most widely distributed group despite having the narrowest host range. The research examined the current distributions of 1,901 crop pests and pathogens, along with historical data on 424 additional species, drawing heavily on CABI’s global records spanning from 1822 to the present. Dr. Timothy Holmes, Head of Technical Solutions at CABI’s Plantwise Knowledge Bank, said: 'By unlocking the potential to understand the distribution of crop pests and diseases, we’re moving one step closer to protecting our ability to feed a growing global population. The hope is to turn data into positive action.' The findings reinforce prior research indicating that climate change is intensifying agricultural pest pressure. The authors describe a global 'cat-and-mouse' dynamic: crops introduced to previously pest-free regions initially thrive, until pests inevitably follow. Professor Sarah Gurr of the University of Exeter added: 'New, virulent variants of pests are constantly evolving. Their emergence is favored by larger pest populations and rapid life cycles, which drive diversifying selection and produce new aggressive genotypes.' 'There is hope,' she continued, 'if robust plant protection strategies and biosecurity measures are implemented—particularly in the developing world, where knowledge and resources are limited. Whether such precautions can slow or stop this process remains to be seen.'

article_content: NASA scientists believe that Europa, one of Jupiter’s moons, is the most likely place beyond Earth to harbor life. Far more promising than Mars — long the focus of U.S. exploration — Europa’s subsurface ocean, thin ice shell, and presence of oxidants make it a stronger candidate for hosting life. NASA has allocated £14.6 million ($25 million) to design probes capable of determining whether life could thrive on Europa. The agency has also revised its exploration strategy, developing a more cost-effective approach to reach the moon. Robert Pappalardo, a planetary scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Pasadena, California, told France 24: 'Europa is the most promising target in terms of habitability. It’s the place we should be exploring now, now that we have a concept mission we believe is both feasible and affordable.' Speaking at the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) annual conference, Pappalardo revealed that the proposed $2 billion Clipper mission would involve collaboration with scientists from Johns Hopkins University in Maryland — pending approval. The Clipper spacecraft would enter Jupiter’s orbit and perform multiple close flybys of Europa, enabling comprehensive study of its surface and subsurface features. If approved, Clipper could launch as early as 2021, arriving at Europa three to six years later. However, NASA announced last year that no funding is currently available for the mission. Instead, the agency plans to send a new Mars rover in 2020, similar to Curiosity — which has been operating on the Red Planet since August 2012 — at a cost of approximately $2.5 billion. The Juno spacecraft arrived at Jupiter in 2016 and is scheduled to be deorbited into the planet in 2017, leaving the U.S. without any active probes in the outer solar system until possibly 2030, when the European Space Agency plans to launch its own Jupiter mission. Europa was first observed by the Voyager 1 and 2 missions in 1979 and later studied in detail by the Galileo orbiter in the 1990s. Alongside Saturn’s moon Enceladus, it is among the top candidates for extraterrestrial habitability. Europa is the sixth-closest moon to Jupiter and the smallest of its four Galilean satellites. Discovered by Galileo Galilei in January 1610, it is named after a Phoenician noblewoman from Greek mythology. With a diameter of 3,100 kilometers, it is slightly smaller than Earth’s Moon, yet the sixth-largest moon in the Solar System and the 15th-largest known object. Europa’s surface is remarkably smooth, with very few impact craters, indicating a geologically young and active crust. Scientists believe it hosts a global subsurface ocean roughly 100 kilometers deep, beneath an icy shell estimated to be 10–30 kilometers thick.

article_content: Sen. Rand Paul announced his bid for a second term in the Senate on Tuesday, launching what will likely be a complex election season as he seeks to retain his seat while preparing for a potential presidential campaign. In a low-key rollout, the Kentucky Republican declined to hold a traditional kick-off event, opting instead for a lengthy press release detailing his local and national policy achievements. In fact, Paul was not in Kentucky on Tuesday; he remained in Washington to vote and speak at a Wall Street Journal event. 'What he decided was that he didn’t need a big rally or much fanfare,' said Doug Stafford, Paul’s senior adviser, on a call with reporters. 'He wanted his record to speak for itself.' The challenge for Paul stems from a Kentucky law that permits candidates to appear on the ballot only once per election cycle. If he runs for president — a decision he said will be made in four to six months — he could face a dilemma on May 17, 2016, Kentucky’s primary day. Should he win the GOP nomination for both offices, the conflict would resurface on Election Day. Paul’s team has not disclosed which path they intend to pursue. 'We haven’t abandoned any option, nor have we settled on any,' Stafford said. Last year, Republican allies in the Kentucky Senate attempted to change the law to allow dual candidacies, but the measure stalled in the Democratic-led House. House Speaker Greg Stumbo, a Democrat who helped block the bill, argued it violated the state constitution’s prohibition on special legislation targeting individuals. 'Where I come from, people think if you can’t decide which office you want, you’re not fit to serve in either one,' he said. U.S. Rep. John Yarmuth, a Democrat representing Louisville, believes the dual candidacy won’t harm Paul’s support among Kentucky voters. 'If you like him, you’ll vote for him. If you don’t, you won’t,' he said. 'It didn’t hurt Paul Ryan or Joe Biden when they ran for Congress while on presidential tickets.' Paul has called the law unfair, comparing it to states without similar restrictions. 'Should people in Minnesota get to vote for their favorite son twice, but not Kentuckians?' he asked in an interview with Salon. 'Eligibility for federal office should be uniform across states.' He argues that the law constitutes an unconstitutional additional qualification beyond the three set by the U.S. Constitution: age (30), citizenship (nine years), and state residency. Legal expert Josh Douglas of the University of Kentucky College of Law doubts Paul’s constitutional argument will succeed. 'States have wide latitude in managing elections,' he said. 'There’s no fundamental right to be a candidate, and this law doesn’t add a qualification — it just sets ballot rules.' One alternative: shifting Kentucky’s GOP presidential primary to a caucus or convention system, which would remove Paul’s name from the ballot. Paul confirmed his team has discussed this with the state GOP, though Stafford emphasized these talks predated Paul’s announcement. Another option: Paul could choose not to file for the Kentucky presidential primary, focusing instead on winning the nomination in other states. The filing deadline is late January 2016 — before the Iowa caucuses — allowing him to gauge his momentum before committing. Yarmuth called this 'probably his best option.' Given that the GOP nominee is typically decided well before May, Kentucky’s primary may not significantly influence the outcome.

article_content: Scientists have named a newly discovered water mite species after global pop icon Jennifer Lopez—not because of any biological similarity, but because her music kept them smiling while writing their research paper. Led by biologist Vladimir Pešić from the University of Montenegro, the team collected the tiny arthropod from a coral reef in the Mona Passage, between Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic, at nearly 70 meters deep—a record depth for its family. They named it Litarachna lopezae as a fun nod to Lopez’s hits like 'I Luh Ya Papi' and 'Ain't It Funny', which played in the background during their work and while they watched the 2014 World Cup. Published in the peer-reviewed journal ZooKeys, the study highlights the species’ habitat in mesophotic coral ecosystems, which are increasingly recognized as rich, underexplored zones of marine biodiversity. While little is known about the mite’s life cycle, its discovery adds to our understanding of deep-water ecosystems—and maybe even proves that great science can happen to the beat of a pop song.

article_content: KISS, the iconic rock band, is set to launch its first-ever Las Vegas residency this November at The Joint inside the Hard Rock Hotel & Casino. The nine-show engagement comes as part of the group’s 40th-anniversary celebration and coincides with their ongoing summer tour alongside Def Leppard. 'What happens in Vegas won’t stay in Vegas — not if we have anything to do with it,' said co-founder Gene Simmons. 'We’re planning to blow the roof off the Hard Rock.' Known for explosive stage productions, KISS promises its most elaborate show yet: massive pyrotechnics, intricate set designs, and a career-spanning setlist — all delivered in an intimate venue seating fewer than 4,000 fans, a stark contrast to their typical stadium crowds. The residency runs three nights per week during the first three weeks of November, offering fans an unprecedented close-up experience with the legendary quartet: Simmons, 64; Stanley, 62; drummer Eric Singer, who joined in 1991; and lead guitarist Tommy Thayer, who has been with the band since 2002. Las Vegas residencies continue to thrive as a lucrative model for enduring musical acts, with recent successes from stars like Britney Spears and Olivia Newton-John. The trend underscores a shift toward curated, high-production concerts in destination venues.

article_content: In a deeply personal farewell, Pope Benedict XVI addressed tens of thousands in St. Peter’s Square, speaking not just as a religious leader but as a man reflecting on a long, often difficult journey. He spoke of 'days of sunshine' and 'rough waters' — moments when, he admitted, it felt like God was silent. Though he didn’t mention scandals directly, his words resonated with many who’ve watched the Church struggle under the weight of abuse cases and internal turmoil during his eight-year reign. With calm dignity, the 85-year-old pontiff thanked clergy across the globe, acknowledged the burden of his role — a life without privacy, devoted entirely to service — and explained his resignation as an act of love, not defeat. 'Loving the Church means having the courage to make tough choices,' he said, emphasizing that stepping down was done with peace, not regret. He made it clear his retirement isn’t an exit from faith, but a return to silence: no more public appearances, no more travel, no more ceremonies. He’ll live in a quiet monastery inside the Vatican, wearing simple white robes and brown shoes, dedicating his days to prayer and books — a welcome return to the scholar he once was. Though he’s stepping away, his legacy lingers. He appointed nearly two-thirds of the cardinals who will choose his successor — a fact that ensures his influence won’t vanish overnight. And while Vatican officials insist he’ll remain in the background, some worry that having two living figures with the title 'Pope' could confuse the faithful. As crowds cheered, sang, and wept, Benedict made his final rounds in the Popemobile, waving through tears. For many, this wasn’t just the end of a papacy — it was the closing of an era. Now, the Church waits, holding its breath, as history prepares to elect its next leader — the first in six centuries to follow a resigned pope.

Ele deixou claro que sua aposentadoria não é uma saída da fé, mas um retorno ao silêncio: mais nenhuma aparição pública, mais viagens, mais cerimônias. article_content: In 2011, the legal struggles of actress Lindsay Lohan and her father Michael Lohan drew renewed public attention — not just because of their individual arrests, but because of the striking parallels between their histories. Over the past decade, both have faced repeated encounters with the justice system, including multiple DUIs, probation violations, and incidents tied to substance use and domestic conflict. Michael Lohan’s criminal record stretches back to 1990, when Lindsay was only four. That year, he was charged with contempt of court following an insider trading investigation. He served jail time and was placed on probation. By 1997, he broke that probation by traveling to California to visit Lindsay during a hospital stay — a move that landed him back behind bars for another year. In 2004, Michael was arrested after a physical altercation outside his son’s birthday party, followed by a DUI and unlicensed driving charge related to a car crash. He spent over two years incarcerated. Then, in July 2010, he was accused of domestic violence against his then-fiancée, Kate Major, in the Hamptons. Although she later withdrew the charges, the incident marked a turning point in public perception. Just weeks before Lindsay’s latest court date in October 2011, Michael was arrested again in Tampa — this time for allegedly becoming violent toward Kate after she refused intimate advances. After being released on bail, he violated a court order by repeatedly calling her, even when police were present. To evade arrest, he reportedly jumped from a third-floor balcony, fracturing his foot. He was hospitalized under police guard and faced new charges including obstruction and violation of a domestic violence injunction. Meanwhile, Lindsay’s own legal journey began in 2006 with a DUI arrest at age 19. She later faced additional charges for possession, driving with a suspended license, and theft of a necklace from a Venice store. Despite court-mandated rehab, community service at the LA County Morgue, and ankle monitoring, her probation was revoked multiple times due to failed drug tests and missed appointments. By October 2011, a judge had ordered her back to jail, setting bail at $100,000, and mandated 16 hours of additional morgue service before her November 2 hearing. While headlines often frame their stories as a tragic family legacy of bad choices, the reality is more complex — involving addiction, mental health, inadequate support systems, and a media culture obsessed with spectacle over solutions.

article_content: A fossil of the largest known platypus ever discovered has been found in Australia’s Riversleigh World Heritage Area. The remains — primarily a single, well-preserved lower molar — suggest the ancient creature, named Obdurodon tharalkooschild, reached nearly one metre in length, roughly twice the size of today’s platypus. Unlike modern platypuses, which lose their teeth as adults and grind food with keratinous pads, Obdurodon tharalkooschild retained powerful, functional teeth. These adaptations likely allowed it to hunt larger prey, including lungfish, frogs, and small turtles, as evidenced by fossils found alongside it at the Two Tree Site. Until now, scientists believed the platypus lineage evolved in a straightforward, linear fashion — gradually shrinking in size and losing teeth over time. This discovery reveals a previously unknown branch on the platypus family tree, showing that some ancient relatives grew much larger than previously thought. The fossil is estimated to be between 5 and 15 million years old, though precise dating is still pending. It was uncovered in freshwater limestone deposits rich with ancient fauna. The species name, Obdurodon tharalkooschild, combines Greek ('lasting tooth') with the name of a figure from an Indigenous Australian Dreamtime story. According to the legend, Tharalkoo, a disobedient duck, gave birth to the first platypus after being transformed by the water-rat Bigoon — a tale that reflects deep cultural connections to this unique animal. Lead researcher Rebecca Pian of the University of New South Wales emphasized the significance of even fragmentary fossils: 'A new platypus species, even one that is highly incomplete, is a very important aid in developing understanding about these fascinating mammals.' Co-authors Dr. Suzanne Hand and Dr. Michael Archer noted that Obdurodon tharalkooschild was likely a fully aquatic predator, thriving in the forested freshwater systems of ancient northern Queensland. Its existence reshapes our view of monotreme evolution, proving greater diversity existed in the past. The platypus remains one of nature’s most extraordinary creatures: it lays eggs, swims with webbed feet, detects prey using electroreception in its bill, and males possess venomous spurs. Despite centuries of study, new discoveries continue to surprise scientists.

Ao contrário dos ornitorrincos modernos, que perdem os dentes na vida adulta e moem alimentos com placas queratinosas, Obdurodon tharalkooschild mantinha dentes poderosos e funcionais. Essas adaptações provavelmente permitiam que ele caçasse presas maiores, incluindo lambaris, rãs e pequenas tartarugas, como evidenciado por fósseis encontrados junto dele no sítio fossilífero Two Tree Site. Até agora, os cientistas acreditavam que a linhagem do ornitorrinco evoluiu de forma linear e direta — gradualmente encolhendo em tamanho e perdendo dentes ao longo do tempo. Esta descoberta revela um ramo anteriormente desconhecido na árvore genealógica do ornitorrinco, mostrando que alguns parentes antigos cresceram muito mais do que se pensava. O fóssil tem uma idade estimada entre 5 e 15 milhões de anos, embora a datação precisa ainda esteja pendente. Foi descoberto em depósitos de calcário de água doce ricos em fauna antiga. O nome da espécie, Obdurodon tharalkooschild, combina o grego ('dente duradouro') com o nome de uma figura de um conto aborígine australiano do Tempo do Sonho. Segundo a lenda, Tharalkoo, um pato desobediente, deu à luz o primeiro ornitorrinco após ser transformado pelo rato-d'água Bigoon — uma história que reflete profundas conexões culturais com este animal único. A pesquisadora principal Rebecca Pian, da Universidade de Nova Gales do Sul, enfatizou a importância mesmo de fósseis fragmentários: 'Uma nova espécie de ornitorrinco, mesmo uma que é altamente incompleta, é um auxílio muito importante para desenvolver o entendimento sobre esses mamíferos fascinantes.' Os coautores Dra. Suzanne Hand e Dr. Michael Archer observaram que Obdurodon tharalkooschild provavelmente era um predador totalmente aquático, vivendo nos sistemas de água doce florestais da antiga Queensland setentrional. Sua existência redefine nossa visão da evolução dos monotremados, provando que houve maior diversidade no passado. O ornitorrinco continua sendo uma das criaturas mais extraordinárias da natureza: ele põe ovos, nada com patas nadadeiras, detecta presas usando eletrorecepção em seu bico e os machos possuem esporões venenosos. Apesar de séculos de estudo, novas descobertas continuam surpreendendo os cientistas.

article_content: If Dave Hockaday hopes to extend his fragile tenure as Leeds United manager, a 4-2 home defeat to Bradford City — Leeds’ first loss in the West Yorkshire derby in 28 years — will do little to help. With another player sent off and fans chanting for his dismissal, the 56-year-old looked isolated amid the chaos of a dramatic, high-stakes match. For 115 seconds, hope flickered. Matt Smith’s 82nd-minute header gave Leeds a slender lead after Luke Murphy’s first-half red card. But within 90 seconds, Bradford turned despair into ecstasy: Billy Knott equalized with a stunning 25-yard strike, and James Hanson headed home the winner moments later. Bradford’s victory marked their first win at Valley Parade in over 80 years — a historic moment for the League One side, who now face MK Dons in the next round after their famous FA Cup upset of Manchester United. Hockaday’s position grows more precarious by the day. Owner Massimo Cellino left the stadium before the final whistle, echoing the growing sentiment among fans that the manager’s time is up. This follows a 4-1 thrashing at Watford, where two players were also sent off. Murphy’s dismissal came after two reckless challenges — the second a knee-high tackle on James Meredith — leaving Leeds with 10 men for over 60 minutes. Yet Hockaday praised his team’s resilience: 'The rest of the team were magnificent to a man.' He admitted the late collapse was cruel: 'Sometimes you have to say, that’s a great strike.' Still, he remained defiant: 'I’m a fighter, not a quitter. We’re devastated, but we believe we can turn this around.' Bradford manager Phil Parkinson hailed his side’s composure: 'It took inspiration from Billy to get us back in — top class. To then win? Brilliant. This is a big moment for Bradford.' With Leeds now winless in five matches and spiraling into turmoil, the pressure on Hockaday is immense — and Saturday’s clash with Bolton may be his last chance to survive.

Com outro jogador expulso e torcedores gritando por sua demissão, o treinador de 56 anos parecia isolado no caos de uma partida dramática e de alto risco. Por 115 segundos, houve esperança. Este é um grande momento para Bradford.' Com o Leeds sem vitórias em cinco partidas e mergulhado no caos, a pressão sobre Hockaday é imensa — e o confronto contra o Bolton neste sábado pode ser sua última chance de sobreviver.

article_content: When I'm in a cranky mood, nothing lifts my spirits quite like watching cute animals make adorable noises while munching on their favorite snacks. Today’s animal star is the porcupine. Here’s an absolutely delightful porcupine named Sid enjoying a banana. Meet Big Ben, a charming fellow munching on a sweet potato — making the sweetest happy eating noises. And here’s a cutie named Rico chomping on peanut butter, banana chips, and pumpkin treats. Sid and Big Ben both live at Wilderness Miracles Wildlife Rehab in Bowdoin, Maine — a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that rehabilitates injured, orphaned, and displaced Maine wildlife. They are currently caring for 15 raccoons, nine porcupines, three mice, two gray squirrels, four chipmunks, three opossums, and five red squirrels. Rico is a resident at the Cincinnati Zoo and Botanical Garden. Big Ben’s hilarious grunts and squeaks reminded me so much of Teddy Bear, Zooniversity’s resident porcupine, whom we featured back in 2014 eating pumpkins for Halloween. article_content: Cast your eye across a lineup of world leaders, and you might see this: man in a dark suit, man in a dark suit, man in a dark suit — and Angela Merkel in a fiery red two-piece. Or perhaps mint green, or electric blue. It doesn’t matter which hue she chooses; Merkel’s colorful power suits have become as iconic in political fashion as Margaret Thatcher’s shoulder pads or Jacqueline Kennedy’s pearls. While Merkel won’t likely grace the front rows of New York, Paris, or London Fashion Week anytime soon, her wardrobe remains as commanding as her politics. But how do women dress to make an impression in the workplace? And how has this changed over time? From the utilitarian khakis of World War II to the romantic princess dresses of the 1950s and the assertive power suits of the 1980s, CNN explores women’s workplace fashion in the 20th century — and the pioneering female designers behind it. "Women have worn tight pencil skirts and high heels at various times — not always practical, but often necessary to be taken seriously," said Rebecca Arnold, professor of fashion history at London’s Courtauld Institute of Art. "For many, workwear is less about fashion and more about mental comfort, fitting in, and appearing respectable." Of course, norms vary by profession. As Arnold notes, "A lawyer dresses differently from a retail worker." Looking back over the past century, workplace fashion mirrors larger social shifts. "From the 1920s onward, women used clothing to negotiate public space — to show how they wanted to be seen," Arnold explained. "In the 1970s, debates raged: Should feminists wear trousers to be taken seriously, or was that too masculine?" Yet workplace fashion rarely follows runway trends. "We still wear shirts cut like men’s, suits modeled after male silhouettes," Arnold said. "Professional dress moves slower than fashion itself." Some of the most transformative pieces in women’s workwear were designed by women: Coco Chanel’s 1920s suit dress, Diane von Furstenberg’s 1970s wrap dress. Yet many top fashion houses remain led by male names — Christian Dior, Yves Saint Laurent, Gianni Versace. "Men have historically been better at marketing themselves and asserting authority over consumers," Arnold observed. "That’s slowly changing — but real progress won’t come until we see more women in leadership roles across all industries."

article_content: By Matt Chorley, MailOnline Political Editor. Published: 10:25 EST, 25 July 2013. Updated: 11:11 EST, 25 July 2013. David Cameron and his wife Samantha boarded an EasyJet flight to Portugal today, as politicians began their summer escapes from Westminster. Downing Street emphasized that the Prime Minister remains in charge, even as he and his three children flew to Faro at 8 a.m. Deputy Prime Minister Nick Clegg traveled to Spain earlier this week, stating that other senior ministers would 'hold the fort' while the two leading figures in the coalition enjoy time overseas. This is not the first time the Prime Minister has taken a budget airline for his annual holiday. In 2011, he was photographed waiting in a departure lounge for a Ryanair flight to Granada. Despite having six weeks to coordinate schedules, both Cameron and Clegg are abroad simultaneously—again. MPs began their summer recess a week ago and are not scheduled to return until early September. Clegg admitted he could not align his family holiday with the Camerons', and other ministers will manage duties in their absence. Last year, the pair faced criticism for taking vacation at the same time, prompting questions about the purpose of the deputy prime minister role if he does not act in the PM's stead. On Tuesday, Clegg was pictured enjoying a drink at a café terrace near his family’s summer home in Olmedo, Valladolid, central Spain. The Cleggs visit Olmedo annually, as it is home to Miriam’s family. Clegg has expressed a desire to travel further afield, joking that now his children are older, he can let them 'lobby against' the usual destination. 'Then I can tell my wife,' he reportedly said, 'Sorry, Miriam—it’s not me, the kids want somewhere less dusty for a change.' It is understood that after returning from Spain, the Cleggs plan a second holiday in France before heading back to Spain. In contrast, the Camerons are enjoying a low-key break in Portugal ahead of their annual trip to Cornwall. They are also reportedly planning a visit to Scotland—during the campaign against Scottish independence. Foreign Secretary William Hague and Home Secretary Theresa May are expected to share responsibility for government operations during the leaders’ absence. Senior aides stressed that Cameron remains fully in command regardless of location. 'The PM is always in charge,' said a Downing Street source. Earlier this month, Clegg told listeners on LBC Radio: 'The Prime Minister and I try, where we can, to avoid traveling at the same time—but there isn't always a perfect match.' He acknowledged a brief overlap this summer, adding: 'We're sort of trying to hand over the baton to each other. We've got other senior ministers—William Hague, the Home Secretary, and others—who can hold the fort during these periods, whether for official reasons or during the recess.'

article_content: Earlier this week, Marina Shifrin became an internet sensation after posting a YouTube video of herself dancing out of her workplace to Kanye West’s hit song 'Gone' — a playful farewell to her job as a content writer at Next Media Animation, a Taiwanese news video production company. Frustrated by the lack of creative freedom in her role, Shifrin’s video has since amassed over 12 million views. Just days later, her former employer responded with its own dancing video — a humorous nod to her viral exit. In honor of Shifrin’s bold and whimsical departure, here are some of the most unforgettable ways people have resigned from their jobs — blending wit, drama, and defiance. Resign with a cake: In April 2023, Chris Holmes, a border force officer at Stansted Airport, baked a stunning carrot cake — packed with coconut, pecans, sultanas, and orange buttercream — inscribed with his resignation message. His thoughtful gesture ensured a warm send-off. 'He leaves with our very best wishes,' said UK Border Force Assistant Director Bill Form. Whether the cake was eaten or archived by HR remains a delicious mystery. Bid adieu with a brass band: In 2011, Joey DeFrancesco, a disgruntled employee at the Providence Renaissance Hotel in Rhode Island, handed his resignation letter to a bewildered manager — then exited the building to the tune of a live brass band. 'I hated them, and they hated me,' DeFrancesco later told HuffPost. 'I knew I had to get one last shot at them.' Take the emergency exit: In 2010, JetBlue flight attendant Steven Slater exploded after a passenger yelled at him for not immediately opening the cabin door upon landing. He announced over the intercom: 'I’ve been in this business 20 years. And that’s it, I’m done.' Then, he grabbed a beer, ripped off his tie, and slid down the emergency chute onto the tarmac before walking to the parking lot. He was later given one year’s probation for criminal mischief and reckless endangerment. The New York Times op-ed: In 2012, Goldman Sachs executive Greg Smith didn’t just quit — he published a blistering op-ed in The New York Times, accusing the firm of becoming 'rotten to the core' and treating clients as 'muppets' to be exploited. His candid critique sparked national debate. He wasn’t alone: In 2008, Andrew Lahde used the Financial Times to publicly dismantle Wall Street giants like Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers as he shuttered his own firm. In front of an entire nation: Long before YouTube, public resignations were rare — unless you were a politician. In 1990, UK Deputy Prime Minister Geoffrey Howe delivered a scathing speech in Parliament, condemning Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher’s European policies and autocratic leadership. Colleagues sat stunned; opposition MPs cheered. Within days, Thatcher was forced from office, her tenure ending in tears.

article_content: The parents of 14-year-old Breck Bednar are suing Surrey Police and Essex Police, alleging failures that contributed to his murder by an online predator. Breck was fatally stabbed by 19-year-old Lewis Daynes, whom he met through an online gaming group playing Battlefield 4. Two months before the killing, Breck’s parents — Barry Bednar and Lorin LaFave, American residents living in Caterham, Surrey — reported to Surrey Police that Daynes was grooming their son online, manipulating his views on religion, family, and education. Despite these warnings, authorities took no preventive action. After Daynes pleaded guilty to the murder, it was revealed that Essex Police may have withheld relevant information about Daynes’ prior conduct. Breck’s mother stated that while her son admired Daynes’ charisma and technical skills, he could not recognize the manipulation behind them. Surrey Police are now under investigation by the Independent Police Complaints Commission for their response to the initial report. Assistant Chief Constable Gavin Stephens confirmed that internal procedures have since been revised to improve information sharing and call handling. Essex Police declined to comment on the pending civil claim. Breck had told his parents he was going to a sleepover before traveling to Daynes’ home in Grays, Essex, where he was killed in a sexually or sadistically motivated attack.

article_content: On February 25, 2013, Commons Speaker John Bercow mistakenly introduced former England rugby star Ben Cohen as 'openly gay' during a speech at ParliOut, Parliament’s LGBTQ+ staff network. The audience erupted in laughter as Cohen quipped, 'Don’t tell my wife!' — a reference to his marriage to Abigail and their five-year-old twin daughters, Harriett and Isabelle. Bercow, visibly embarrassed, immediately apologized, stating, 'I am not in favour of outing people against their will — that was an ignorant outing, and I apologize to Ben.' He clarified that Cohen, a 57-cap international rugby player, had dedicated his post-retirement years to combating homophobic bullying through his StandUP Foundation. Cohen, who has been featured on the covers of gay magazines and named Gay Times’ Sports Personality of the Year in 2008, took the slip in stride. He later posted a photo of himself with Bercow on Facebook, calling the experience a 'great honour.' However, some online commentators speculated that Bercow had confused Ben Cohen with Benjamin Cohen, the openly gay founder of Pink News. While Ben Cohen has long been embraced as a gay icon due to his advocacy and visibility, he identifies as a heterosexual man married to a woman. In a separate but unrelated matter, Sally Bercow, John’s wife, is facing a £50,000 defamation lawsuit from Lord McAlpine over a tweet she posted implying he was linked to a child abuse scandal — a claim later proven false. She has dismissed the case as 'politically motivated' and accused McAlpine’s legal team of being 'ambulance chasers.'

article_content: Relatives of a deceased man from Washington State were horrified on Monday when they opened the casket at his funeral to say their final goodbyes — only to discover another man’s body inside. The situation grew even more distressing when they noticed the stranger had a plastic bag over his head. The mix-up occurred at Brown Mortuary in Longview, approximately 80 miles north of Portland, Oregon. The facility had taken custody of Jerry Moon’s body following his death, and around the same time, also received the body of a 97-year-old man who had passed away in hospice care. The two bodies were inadvertently swapped. 'This makes me feel like he was treated as a number, not a person,' said Cheryl Moon, Jerry’s daughter, to KIROTV.com. At the conclusion of the funeral service, the family opened the casket. 'I turned around and said to myself three times, 'That’s not him, that’s not him, that’s not him,'' recalled Jerry’s son, Randy Moon. Inside the casket was the 97-year-old man — dressed in Jerry Moon’s clothing, with a photograph of Moon’s wife tucked beneath the pillow. Compounding the tragedy, Jerry Moon had a deep fear of cremation. Because of the error, the mortuary cremated his body, mistakenly believing it was the other man’s. Brown Mortuary, operated by Houston-based Service Corporation International (SCI), declined to comment on the incident, citing directives from its parent company. SCI manages roughly 1,400 funeral homes and 400 cemeteries across the United States and Canada. 'The only thing I can say is we know where he really is,' Randy Moon said. 'We’re a believing family, and we believe he is in heaven.'

article_content: Debbie Rowe, Michael Jackson’s former wife and mother of his two eldest children, is scheduled to testify in the AEG Live wrongful death trial this week. Her testimony is expected to focus on Jackson’s pattern of drug use during the 1990s — a period when she traveled with him, married him, and gave birth to their children. She will appear after an economic expert finishes detailing the financial support Jackson would have provided his mother and three children had he survived. Randy Jackson, Michael’s youngest brother, previously testified that he and their father were denied entry to Jackson’s rented home on Carolwood Drive in the weeks before his death. Randy said he was alarmed by reports that Michael looked unwell, wasn’t eating, and was deeply entangled in painkiller dependency. He tried repeatedly to stage interventions — in places like Taiwan, Las Vegas, and Neverland Ranch — urging his brother to seek rehab. But Michael refused, fearing judgment and unwilling to let his family see him in such a state. The lawsuit against AEG Live claims the concert promoter negligently hired Dr. Conrad Murray — paying him $150,000 per month — who then supplied Jackson with nightly propofol infusions to treat insomnia during rehearsals for the 'This Is It' tour. Jackson’s attorneys argue Murray was financially dependent on the job and couldn’t refuse the singer’s demands. AEG Live counters that Jackson personally chose Murray and kept his medical treatment private, leaving the company unaware of the risks. Multiple witnesses, including Jackson’s makeup artist and show director, described visible signs of physical deterioration in the months before his death. Randy Jackson recalled one incident in 2005 when his brother had a severe reaction to a sedative at a Beverly Hills home; a nearby doctor was called to treat him. He also said he suspected their nanny, Grace Rwaramba, of enabling Jackson’s drug use, and asked his sister Rebbie to keep close watch on him during the 2004 child abuse trial. Though Jackson publicly acknowledged his addiction during the 1993 Dangerous tour hiatus, his legal team maintains he often went extended periods without drugs. They attribute his reliance on painkillers and sedatives to decades of physical trauma — including severe scalp burns from a 1984 Pepsi ad shoot and repeated onstage injuries. Experts say the nightly propofol use severely disrupted his sleep cycle, accelerating his decline. The trial, now entering its 16th week, continues with jurors reviewing video clips of Randy Jackson’s emotional testimony — including the infamous ‘pajama day’ when Michael arrived late to court dressed in pajamas. Randy clarified it wasn’t due to a fall, as Jackson claimed, but because he simply didn’t want to face the courtroom. The case could extend into late September.

article_content: Carol Tsoi, 64, of Wigan, Greater Manchester, died by suicide hours before her husband, Kam Tsoi, was due to appear in court facing historic sex offense charges involving four young girls. An inquest revealed she had been deeply anxious about the outcome of the trial — a fear compounded by pre-existing physical and mental health struggles and recent personal losses. Mrs. Tsoi, who had been treated for depression following the deaths of her father and beloved pet dog Izzy, also battled diabetes, asthma, worsening arthritis (with a pending hip transplant), bowel complications, and intermittent alcohol dependence. Despite undergoing a gastric band procedure to manage her weight, her health continued to decline. On October 12, 2013, the family spent the day together attending a car boot sale. Mrs. Tsoi appeared in good spirits that morning. Later that evening, she retired early to her bedroom, declined dinner, and locked the door from within. Her son Michael, who was staying overnight, discovered her the next morning lying face down beside her bed. He had to force the door open after receiving no response to his calls. A post-mortem examination by Dr. Stephen Wells confirmed death by drug overdose. Police found no signs of foul play. Notably, Mrs. Tsoi had told her GP she intended to attend the trial to support her husband and had expressed no prior thoughts of self-harm. Shortly after her death, Mr. Tsoi was acquitted of all nine charges in Liverpool Crown Court. Michael Tsoi described his mother as having endured 'one thing after another' without time to recover. 'She was terrified about the court case and what may happen. I think she had had enough,' he said at the inquest.

article_content: Did Billy Crystal save the Oscars? Though no major blockbusters dominated the nominations, the 84th Academy Awards managed a modest uptick in viewership, drawing 39.3 million people on ABC — a 4% increase from 2011. Still, the real story wasn’t the Oscars’ gain, but the Grammys’ breakthrough: earlier this month, CBS’s music awards pulled in 39.9 million viewers, narrowly beating the Oscars for the first time since Nielsen began tracking in 1992. Among adults aged 18–49, the gap was even clearer: the Grammys scored a 14.1 rating versus the Oscars’ 11.7. Looking back, Oscar viewership has swung widely over the decades — from the record-breaking 55.2 million who watched 'Titanic' in 1998, to the low point of 32 million during 'No Country for Old Men' in 2008. Meanwhile, other Sunday night shows felt the impact: CBS’s 'The Amazing Race' dropped 25%, and NBC’s 'Celebrity Apprentice' plunged 31%, likely because audiences chose the Oscars over reality TV — even if it meant watching Donald Trump’s latest spectacle.

Entre adultos de 18 a 49 anos, a diferença foi ainda mais clara: os Grammys tiveram uma classificação de 14,1 contra os 11,7 dos Oscars.
